body.text: Kazakhs are interested in the development of their country, but some believe that efforts to change the mind of their government on key issues are futile. This was one of the main findings of a survey published on November 12 by the Kazakh public opinion polling company Demoscope.

Participation in referendums and elections was by far the most common form of political engagement, with appeals to government bodies a distant second. Just under half of respondents did not report participating in any civic or political activities at all.

The survey results come as human rights and civil society organizations have accused Kazakhstan in 2026 of muzzling the press and generally hindering civic action in the country, prosecuting multiple activists and journalists this year alone.

The Demoscope survey, “Assessment of Political Participation among Citizens of Kazakhstan,” was conducted among 1,100 people from all 17 regions of Kazakhstan, as well as the cities of Astana, Almaty, and Shymkent.

While the survey found that 52.4 percent of the public were interested in the social and political development of Kazakhstan, only 48.2 percent of respondents believed that citizens could exert some degree of influence on decisions made by the authorities.

Just over 54 percent stated that they would not challenge the government over decisions that could affect their well-being. Of these, 31 percent said they would refrain from taking action because they considered it “pointless.”

While between 20.8 and 25.8 percent attributed their lack of political engagement to a lack of interest in politics, time, or simply not finding any causes that required their participation, close to a third considered efforts to change political decisions futile. At the same time, 27.5 percent said that citizens had no means of exerting real influence over political decision-making in the country.

This distrust of the political system was also reflected in the number of respondents who reported voting, with only 44.7 percent stating that they had participated in an election or referendum within the past year. These findings are considerably lower than the turnout figures recorded during the March referendum or the August parliamentary elections this year, both of which had officially reported participation rates of over 70 percent. This discrepancy was noted directly by Demoscope.

Meanwhile, all other forms of political participation were considerably less common, with fewer than 10 percent reporting that they had sent an appeal to the government. Even lower were the numbers of citizens who had participated in civic initiatives or peaceful assemblies, with just 1.3 and 1.2 percent reporting such activities, respectively.

This is not a new development in Kazakhstan but rather one that has been unfolding since the Qandy Qantar – “Bloody January” – unrest in 2022. It was also evident during last year’s Independence Day protest, which The Diplomat reported was attended mostly by pensioners, several of whom expressed fears of arrest for their participation.

During 2026, Kazakhstan has seen a string of arrests and prosecutions of bloggers, civil activists, and journalists. In April alone, 19 activists were found guilty of inciting interethnic discord following a protest the previous year calling for the release of ethnic Kazakhs facing prosecution in Xinjiang, China. Eleven of the defendants were given five-year prison sentences, while the rest received lighter sentences involving restricted freedom.

October 2026 saw another large-scale case go to trial, with activist Sanzhar Bokayev accused of disseminating false information. His supporters, however, suspect that the case is intended to silence his criticism of the government. Similar charges have also been used this year to sentence journalists, including the former editor of Orda.kz Gulnara Bazhkenova.

Cases like these, along with instances of civil activists having their homes raided by police, have led to criticism from multiple human rights organizations. Amnesty International has particularly focused on the activists jailed for protesting in support of Kazakhs imprisoned in China, calling the sentences for peaceful assembly a “travesty for justice.”

Similar criticism has also come from Kazakhstan’s International Bureau for Human Rights and Rule of Law. Based on its analysis of cases involving activists during 2026, the bureau stated that “individuals who seek to exercise their freedom of peaceful assembly, face substantial legal and operational risks.”

Despite the crackdown on activism in recent years, Demoscope still found that younger generations in particular were prepared to challenge the government, if necessary. In fact, 54.2 percent of respondents aged 18-29 stated that they would be willing to take action if government decisions were made that negatively affected their lives.

Despite the majority of Kazakhs expressing interest in the country’s political development, the ongoing prosecution of activists appears to be affecting citizens’ willingness to protest against their government. With younger generations showing a greater readiness to protest, the coming years will show whether this willingness can translate into meaningful civic action or will fade with time.
